title: A 1936-1999 global temperature link predicted the 2000-2025 mean discharge of six Eurasian Arctic rivers to within 1%, but year-to-year changes did not follow temperature
abstract: Peterson et al. (2002) related the combined annual discharge of the six largest Eurasian Arctic rivers to global mean temperature (0.007 Sv, or 221 km3/yr, per degree C) for 1936-1999. We did a planned out-of-sample test. We fitted the relation on 1936-1999 ArcticGRO data (54 years) and GISTEMP v4, kept it frozen, and compared it with 2000-2025 discharge (25 years), when warming was much faster. The observed 2000-2025 mean was 1,967 km3/yr. The frozen fit predicted 1,949 km3/yr (95% interval 1,867-2,032). The published slope gave a mean error of -0.4 km3/yr. The realized sensitivity was 220 km3/yr per degree C (95% interval 128-307). The fit had 51% less squared error than the 1936-1999 mean. A frozen linear time trend predicted 1,904 km3/yr, which is also inside its interval, and the error difference between the two models was not resolved. Year-to-year discharge changes did not follow year-to-year temperature changes in either period, so the link is multi-decadal and does not prove a cause. The result held in 8 of 9 robustness tests; a regional Eurasian land temperature model under-predicted. Five of six rivers were inside their intervals; the Northern Dvina was over-predicted. The NAO correlation was weak (r = 0.25) in both periods. Limits: gaps filled in the ArcticGRO record, Kolyma and Pechora reconstructions, and provisional Russian data after 2017. Code, plan, derived annual tables, results and figures are included; raw daily data are downloaded by script.
